nodeData.note: Sucking pests, caterpillars, beetles, fruit flies, soil and storage pests, organic weed control and protecting pollinators.

children.note: Small insects and mites that pierce plant tissue and suck sap. They weaken plants, spread viruses and leave sticky honeydew; most outbreaks are man-made, so organic control starts with protecting natural enemies.

Caterpillars are the larvae of moths (order Lepidoptera) and chew leaves, stems, fruit and cobs. Many can be managed organically by catching them young: monitor moths, protect egg parasitoids and use Bt, viruses and push–pull.

Chewing beetles and snouted weevils attack berries, corms, roots, leaves and stored grain. This map covers the main ones in coffee, banana, sweet potato, vegetables and pulses, plus the Antestia bug of coffee, with organic ways to keep them below damaging levels.

Tephritid fruit flies lay eggs inside fruit and vegetables, and their maggots rot the crop from within. The Oriental fruit fly has spread across Africa since 2003. Organic control works best when neighbours act together across a whole area.

Termites, white grubs, cutworms, wireworms, millipedes, mole crickets, slugs, snails and burrowing rodents that attack seed and roots. How to recognise them and control them with organic methods: biological agents, botanicals, field practices, traps and predators.
Insects, moulds and aflatoxin that attack grain and beans after harvest, and the organic ways to stop them: harvest and drying, airtight storage, inert dusts, botanicals, clean stores and monitoring.

Weeds are managed, not eradicated, on an organic farm. The aim is to stop them hurting yield during the crop's sensitive window and to shrink the weed seed bank year by year — using prevention, smart timing, soil cover, tools and living plants instead of synthetic herbicides.

Bees and other pollinators turn flowers into fruit and seed, and the same diverse habitat that feeds them also feeds the natural enemies of pests. Protecting them raises yields and quality, and beekeeping adds farm income.

nodeData.note: Small insects and mites that pierce plant tissue and suck sap. They weaken plants, spread viruses and leave sticky honeydew; most outbreaks are man-made, so organic control starts with protecting natural enemies.

children.note: What these pests have in common and why they matter.
Aphids, whiteflies, mealybugs, scales, leafhoppers and psyllids (bugs, order Hemiptera) push a needle-like stylet into the phloem; thrips rasp cells; mites pierce single leaf cells.

manas.q: How do sucking pests feed?

children.note: Phloem feeders excrete sugary honeydew. A black sooty mould grows on it, blocking light and spoiling fruit; ants farm the honeydew and guard the pests.

manas.q: What causes black sooty mould on leaves?

children.note: Many sucking pests carry plant viruses from plant to plant. Often the virus does far more damage than the feeding itself, and even a few insects can spread it.
Short life cycles (often 1–3 weeks in warm weather) and, in aphids, live birth without mating let numbers explode within days.
Many become serious only after broad-spectrum sprays kill their natural enemies, or when plants are stressed or overfed with nitrogen.

manas.q: Why are many sucking pests called 'secondary pests'?

children.note: Soft, pear-shaped insects (family Aphididae) on almost all crops, e.g. Aphis gossypii, Myzus persicae, Brevicoryne brassicae on cabbage, black bean aphid Aphis fabae.
1–4 mm, green, black, grey or pink, in colonies on shoot tips and leaf undersides. Two small tubes (cornicles) at the rear; winged forms appear when crowded.

manas.q: What feature at the rear helps identify an aphid?

children.note: Curled, puckered young leaves, stunted shoots, honeydew, sooty mould and white cast skins. Cabbage aphids form grey waxy clusters inside heads.

Aphids spread many viruses, e.g. bean common mosaic, potato virus Y, cucumber mosaic and groundnut rosette. Some are picked up in seconds, so sprays cannot stop them; barriers and clean seed matter more.

manas.q: Name two viruses spread by aphids.

children.note: Ants protect aphid colonies from ladybirds and parasitoids. Controlling ants (sticky bands on stems, removing nests) lets natural enemies work.
Tiny moth-like bugs: Bemisia tabaci (tropics, field crops) and greenhouse whitefly Trialeurodes vaporariorum. Major pests of tomato, cassava, beans, cotton and cucurbits.
Adults about 1–2 mm with white powdery wings, flying up in a cloud when the plant is shaken. Flat, scale-like nymphs sit on leaf undersides.

manas.q: Where do whitefly nymphs live on the plant?

children.note: Yellowing, honeydew and sooty mould; heavy feeding weakens plants and causes uneven ripening of tomato.
B. tabaci spreads begomoviruses such as tomato yellow leaf curl and cassava mosaic, plus cassava brown streak (an ipomovirus). Virus loss often far exceeds feeding damage.

manas.q: Which whitefly spreads tomato yellow leaf curl virus?

children.note: B. tabaci has developed resistance to many synthetic insecticides, one reason biological and cultural control are important.
Slender insects (order Thysanoptera), 1–2 mm, with fringed wings. They rasp surface cells and suck out the contents; eggs are inserted in tissue and pupae drop to the soil.
Key pest of onion, leek, garlic and cabbage. Causes silvery-white streaks on onion leaves; worst in hot, dry weather.

manas.q: Which thrips species damages onions most?

children.note: Frankliniella occidentalis, a worldwide invasive pest of flowers, beans, tomato and capsicum; important in Kenya's flower and French bean exports. Hides deep in flowers.

links.label: 📄 Source: Annu. Rev. Entomol. 2020 (western flower thrips)

children.note: Feeds on young leaves of chilli, capsicum, mango and citrus, causing upward leaf curl ('murda' complex in India with mites) and brown corky scars.
Silvery patches with tiny black dots (droppings), distorted leaves and flowers, scarred or bronzed fruit and pods. Check by tapping flowers over white paper.

manas.q: What do silvery patches with black dots on leaves suggest?

children.note: Thrips spread tomato spotted wilt virus and related tospoviruses. Only thrips that fed on an infected plant as young larvae can transmit it as adults.

manas.q: Which virus group is spread by thrips?

children.note: Not insects but tiny eight-legged arachnids, mainly the two-spotted spider mite Tetranychus urticae and red spider mites. Pests of tomato, beans, roses, cucurbits and cassava.
Barely visible (about 0.5 mm) moving dots on leaf undersides; a hand lens shows eggs and two dark spots on the body. Fine silk webbing in bad attacks.

manas.q: Are spider mites insects?

children.note: Fine yellow-white speckling (stippling), then bronzed, dry leaves that drop. Webbing over shoot tips means a heavy infestation.
Mites multiply fastest in hot, dry weather and on dusty plants by roadsides; drought-stressed plants suffer most.

manas.q: Which weather favours spider mite outbreaks?

children.note: Some pyrethroids and other broad-spectrum sprays kill predatory mites but not spider mites, often causing worse outbreaks afterwards.
Soft insects covered in white wax (family Pseudococcidae), in cracks, leaf bases, roots and fruit. Pests of papaya, cassava, coffee, citrus, mango and ornamentals.
Paracoccus marginatus, from Central America, arrived in coastal Kenya around 2016 and spread inland, attacking papaya and over 200 other plant species.

manas.q: Where is the papaya mealybug originally from?

children.note: White cottony clusters on fruit, leaves and stems; yellowing, leaf curl, fruit drop, honeydew, sooty mould and heavy ant activity.
In India, release of the tiny wasp Acerophagus papayae controlled papaya mealybug within about five months of release in 2010, with large economic benefits.

manas.q: Which parasitoid wasp controls papaya mealybug?

children.note: The waxy coat repels water-based sprays, so contact products work poorly unless mixed with a wetter or applied with pressure.
Immobile bugs under a wax or hard shell (soft scales and armoured scales). Pests of citrus, mango, coffee, tea and ornamentals.
Small bumps 1–5 mm stuck to stems, leaves and fruit; lift with a fingernail to see the insect. Only the tiny 'crawler' stage moves.

manas.q: Which life stage of scale insects can move?

children.note: Crawlers are unprotected, so oil or soap sprays work best when crawlers are out; check with double-sided tape round a twig.
Wedge-shaped, fast-jumping bugs (family Cicadellidae), e.g. cotton jassid Amrasca biguttula on cotton, okra and brinjal.
Leaf edges turn yellow then red-brown and curl downward ('hopper burn') from toxic saliva. Insects run sideways when disturbed.

manas.q: What is 'hopper burn'?

children.note: Leafhoppers spread maize streak virus (Cicadulina spp.) in Africa and phytoplasma diseases such as little leaf of brinjal in India.
Small jumping plant lice (Psylloidea) that suck sap and can carry bacteria.
The African citrus psyllid Trioza erytreae and the Asian citrus psyllid Diaphorina citri spread the bacteria that cause citrus greening, which has no cure.

manas.q: Which disease do citrus psyllids spread?

children.note: Pits or bumps (galls) on young citrus leaves, curled shoots, white waxy threads and honeydew.
Most sucking pest outbreaks are caused by conditions on the farm, which the farmer can change.
Broad-spectrum insecticides kill ladybirds, lacewings, parasitoids and predatory mites faster than the pests, which then rebound.

manas.q: What is the most common cause of sucking pest outbreaks after spraying?

children.note: Heavy nitrogen fertiliser or fresh manure makes soft, sappy growth rich in amino acids; aphids, whiteflies and mites breed faster on it.

manas.q: How does excess nitrogen affect aphids?

children.note: Water-stressed plants favour mites and thrips; good mulching and irrigation reduce attacks.
Dust on leaves (from roads or dry tillage) harms predatory mites and parasitoids and favours spider mites and scales.
Large single-crop blocks with no flowering plants give enemies no food or shelter; ants guarding honeydew producers keep enemies away.
Finding pests early makes organic control much easier.
Check leaf undersides, shoot tips and flowers of 10–20 plants across the field each week; use a 10× hand lens for mites and thrips.
Yellow traps catch whiteflies, aphids, leafhoppers and some thrips; blue traps attract thrips best. Use them to see when numbers rise.

manas.q: Which sticky trap colour is best for thrips?

children.note: Note mummified (parasitised) aphids, ladybird larvae and predatory mites; if enemies are rising, wait before treating.
Combine prevention, natural enemies and gentle sprays; no single method is enough.
Stop pests building up in the first place.
Feed plants with compost and balanced organic manures rather than heavy nitrogen; healthy, unforced growth is less attractive to sap feeders.
Raise seedlings under insect-proof net (about 50 mesh or finer for whitefly) so they reach the field free of pests and viruses.

manas.q: Why raise seedlings under insect netting?

children.note: Silver or reflective plastic mulch confuses landing aphids, whiteflies and thrips and delays virus infection in young crops.
Tall border rows of maize or sorghum slow aphid and whitefly entry; remove weeds and old crop residues that host pests and viruses.
A hard spray of water washes off aphids and mites, breaks webs and removes dust; useful on small plots and in dry weather.
Protect and, where available, release the enemies of sucking pests.
Ladybirds, lacewing larvae, hoverfly larvae, predatory bugs (e.g. Orius for thrips) and spiders eat large numbers of aphids, whiteflies and thrips.
Phytoseiulus persimilis eats spider mites; Neoseiulus/Amblyseius species eat thrips, whitefly eggs and mites. Widely used in greenhouses, including Kenyan flower farms.

manas.q: Which predatory mite specialises on spider mites?

children.note: Encarsia and Eretmocerus parasitise whiteflies; Aphidius parasitises aphids (look for bronze 'mummies'); Acerophagus papayae attacks papaya mealybug.
Flowering borders (coriander, sunflower, marigold, buckwheat) feed adult parasitoids and hoverflies with nectar and pollen.
Beneficial fungi infect and kill sucking pests; they need humidity and should not be mixed with fungicides.
Fungus that grows over aphids, whiteflies, scales and mealybugs, leaving them covered in white mould. Works best at high humidity.

manas.q: Which fungus covers dead whiteflies and aphids in white mould?

children.note: Wide-host fungus used against whiteflies, thrips and aphids; spores stick to the insect, germinate and grow inside it.
Spray in the evening onto leaf undersides, repeat every 5–7 days during attacks, and keep copper and other fungicides away from the spray tank.
Soft products that kill on contact; cover leaf undersides thoroughly.
Neem seed extract or oil (azadirachtin) repels and disrupts moulting of aphids, whiteflies and thrips; slow-acting, so start early. Allowed in most organic standards.

manas.q: How does neem act on sucking pests?

children.note: Potassium soap dissolves the soft cuticle of aphids, mealybug crawlers and whitefly nymphs. Must hit the pest; no residual effect; test on a few leaves first.
Mineral or plant oils smother scales, mites and eggs. Avoid spraying in hot midday sun or on water-stressed plants to prevent leaf burn.
Synthetic insecticides such as neonicotinoids, organophosphates and pyrethroids are not permitted under organic certification.

manas.q: Are neonicotinoids allowed in organic farming?

children.note: Common mistakes that make sucking pests worse.
Spraying on a fixed schedule, especially broad-spectrum products, wipes out natural enemies and selects resistant pests.
Heavy urea or fresh poultry manure top-dressing brings on aphid and whitefly flare-ups.
Old tomato, cassava or cucurbit fields left standing act as virus and whitefly reservoirs for new plantings.

nodeData.note: Caterpillars are the larvae of moths (order Lepidoptera) and chew leaves, stems, fruit and cobs. Many can be managed organically by catching them young: monitor moths, protect egg parasitoids and use Bt, viruses and push–pull.

children.note: Life cycle and why timing matters.
Egg → several caterpillar stages (instars) → pupa (often in soil) → moth. Moths fly at night and lay eggs; only the caterpillars damage crops.

manas.q: Which life stage of a moth damages crops?

children.note: Small caterpillars are exposed and sensitive to Bt, neem and viruses; large ones feed hidden in whorls, stems or fruit and are hard to reach.

manas.q: Why target young caterpillars?

children.note: Ants, earwigs, birds, parasitoids and diseases kill most eggs and larvae in fields that are not sprayed with broad-spectrum insecticides.
Spodoptera frugiperda, a moth from the Americas, now a major maize pest in Africa and Asia; also attacks sorghum, rice and many other crops.
First officially reported in West and Central Africa in early 2016, then spread across sub-Saharan Africa (Kenya by 2017) and into Asia, including India in 2018.

manas.q: When was fall armyworm first reported in Africa?

children.note: Mature larvae have a pale inverted 'Y' on the dark head and four black dots forming a square on the second-last body segment.

manas.q: Which two marks identify a fall armyworm larva?

children.note: Small 'windowpanes' on young leaves, then ragged holes, and wet sawdust-like droppings (frass) in the whorl; later larvae bore into cobs.
Females lay egg masses of 100–200 eggs covered with grey-pink scales, usually under leaves; moths fly long distances at night.

manas.q: How are fall armyworm egg masses protected?

children.note: Larvae are cannibalistic, so often only one large larva survives in each whorl — useful when hand-picking.
Small moth from South America, reached Spain in 2006 and has since spread across Africa (including Kenya) and Asia; devastating on tomato, also potato and nightshades.
Pale irregular mines (blotches) in leaves with dark frass inside, mines in stems, and small holes with frass at the calyx of green and ripe fruit.

manas.q: How do Tuta absoluta mines differ from simple leaf holes?

children.topic: Why it is hard to control
children.note: Larvae feed inside leaves and fruit, many generations occur per year, and it has evolved resistance to many insecticides.
Without control, losses in tomato can reach total crop failure, especially in warm greenhouses and dry seasons.
Plutella xylostella, the main caterpillar pest of cabbage, kale (sukuma wiki), cauliflower and other brassicas worldwide.
Small green larvae (up to 1 cm), pointed at both ends, wriggle backwards and drop on a silk thread when touched; moths show a diamond pattern on the back.

manas.q: How does a diamondback larva react when touched?

children.note: Young larvae make 'windows' in leaves (only the clear surface remains); later, many small holes and damaged growing points.
It was the first insect to develop resistance to Bt sprays in the field and resists many chemicals, so rotate and combine methods.

manas.q: Which caterpillar first evolved resistance to Bt sprays in the field?

children.note: Helicoverpa armigera, a polyphagous moth larva on tomato, cotton, chickpea, pigeonpea, maize, beans and flowers.
Larvae vary from green to brown with pale side stripes and short hairs; they bore round holes into fruit, pods and bolls.
Neat round holes in tomato fruit or pods with the larva half-inside; damaged fruit rots. One larva can damage several fruits.

manas.q: What sign shows African bollworm in tomato?

children.note: Helicoverpa nucleopolyhedrovirus kills only this pest; infected larvae become limp and hang from plants. Commercial NPV products are used in India and other countries.
Larvae that tunnel inside cereal stems: Busseola fusca (African, highlands) and Chilo partellus (spotted stemborer from Asia, lowlands).
Rows of 'shot holes' on unrolling leaves, dead heart in young plants, tunnels and frass in stems, broken stalks and damaged cobs.

manas.q: What is 'dead heart' in maize?

children.note: Cotesia flavipes was introduced to East Africa from Asia by icipe against Chilo partellus; native Cotesia sesamiae attacks Busseola.
Larvae survive the dry season in old stalks; chop, compost or use stalks as feed before the next season.
Agrotis species, grey-brown fat larvae that hide in the soil by day and cut seedlings at the base at night.
Seedlings cut off at soil level overnight; dig gently around the stump to find a C-shaped curled larva.

manas.q: How do cutworm larvae look when disturbed?

children.note: Plough early to expose larvae to birds, keep fields weed-free before planting, use collars around transplants and handpick at night.
Thaumatotibia leucotreta, an African moth whose larvae bore into fruits: citrus, avocado, capsicum, chilli, macadamia, roses and cotton bolls.
The EU treats it as a regulated quarantine pest; a single intercepted larva in capsicum, chilli, roses or citrus can lead to consignment rejection and stricter checks on Kenya's exports.

manas.q: Why is false codling moth so important for exporters?

children.note: Small entry hole with brown frass on fruit, early ripening or fruit drop; larvae pink when mature. Damage is often hidden until packing.
Orchard sanitation (collect and destroy fallen fruit weekly), pheromone monitoring, mating disruption, granulovirus (CrleGV) and egg parasitoids.
Know when moths arrive and when eggs hatch so control hits young larvae.
Lures release the female sex scent and catch male moths. Rising catches warn that egg-laying has started; one lure per pest species.

manas.q: Which sex of moth is caught in pheromone traps?

children.note: Walk a W across the field and check 10 plants at each of 5 points (50 plants); record % plants with fresh damage or larvae.
Follow local extension thresholds and act when fresh damage on young plants keeps rising, not at the first larva seen; maize can tolerate some leaf damage without yield loss.
Combine cultural methods, biological control and selective sprays.
Field practices that reduce attacks before any spray.
Maize intercropped with desmodium (repels moths: push) and bordered by Napier or Brachiaria grass (attracts them: pull). Developed by icipe in Kenya for stemborers and Striga.

manas.q: In push–pull, which plant repels and which attracts moths?

children.note: In drier parts of Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania, climate-adapted push–pull plots had about 83% fewer FAW larvae and 2.7 times the maize yield of monocrops.
Plant with the first rains and at the same time as neighbours, so maize grows past the vulnerable whorl stage before pest numbers peak.
Maize–legume intercrops, healthy soil with organic matter and natural habitat around fields help reduce FAW and favour enemies.
Nets and screened greenhouses keep Tuta, diamondback moth and bollworm out of nurseries and protected crops; keep doors double-closed.
Many pheromone or light traps per hectare (with water-and-oil pans for Tuta) remove large numbers of males; works best in closed greenhouses.
Cheap and effective on small farms.
Crush egg masses and larvae in the whorl, pick off bored fruit and destroy them. Most useful in the first 3–4 weeks after planting.

manas.q: When is handpicking fall armyworm most useful?

children.topic: Ash, sand or soil in the whorl
children.note: A traditional African practice against FAW. Some farmers report benefit, but evidence from proper trials is limited and mixed; treat it as an option to test, not a proven cure.

manas.q: Is ash in the maize whorl a proven FAW control?

children.note: Collect bored tomatoes, citrus or capsicum that drop and bury them deeply or seal in bags in the sun.
Living enemies and their products.
Tiny wasps that lay eggs in moth eggs, turning them black. Released as 'Tricho-cards' in India and elsewhere against bollworm, stemborers and Tuta.

manas.q: What colour do moth eggs turn when Trichogramma parasitises them?

children.note: Main egg parasitoid of fall armyworm in the Americas; found already present in at least five African countries, offering scope for releases.
Cotesia icipe, a native African wasp, parasitises FAW larvae and Cotesia flavipes attacks stemborers; ants and earwigs also eat many eggs and young larvae.
Bacterial spray (subsp. kurstaki or aizawai) that kills caterpillars that eat treated leaves; harmless to people and most beneficials. Allowed in organic.

manas.q: How does a caterpillar get killed by Bt?

children.note: Nucleopolyhedroviruses (e.g. SfMNPV for FAW, HearNPV for bollworm) and granuloviruses kill only their target species; spray in the evening as sunlight breaks them down.
Insect-killing fungi used against FAW larvae and pupae in the soil; results depend on humidity and good coverage.
Plant-based and organic-allowed sprays.
Neem extract deters egg-laying and feeding and disrupts larval moulting; aim it into the whorl or on young larvae.
Made by a soil bacterium (Saccharopolyspora spinosa) and allowed in many organic standards; effective on caterpillars and thrips but toxic to bees when wet — spray in the evening.
Synthetic insecticides such as pyrethroids, emamectin benzoate, chlorantraniliprole and organophosphates are not permitted in certified organic farming.
Mistakes that make caterpillar problems worse.
Late sprays on big larvae hidden in whorls, stems or fruit waste money; target eggs and young larvae.
Rushed broad-spectrum spraying against FAW kills natural enemies and harms health without solving the problem.
Repeated use of one mode of action, even Bt or spinosad, builds resistance; rotate and combine methods.

nodeData.note: Chewing beetles and snouted weevils attack berries, corms, roots, leaves and stored grain. This map covers the main ones in coffee, banana, sweet potato, vegetables and pulses, plus the Antestia bug of coffee, with organic ways to keep them below damaging levels.

children.note: Getting the insect group right decides which control will work, so look closely before acting.
Beetles have hardened front wings (elytra) that meet in a straight line down the back, and chewing mouthparts that bite holes in leaves, seeds or fruit.

manas.q: How can you tell a beetle from a true bug by its wings?

children.note: Weevils are beetles whose head is drawn out into a snout with tiny jaws at the tip; their larvae are pale, legless grubs that feed hidden inside plant tissue.

manas.q: What body feature marks a weevil?

children.note: True bugs such as Antestia pierce plant tissue with a needle-like beak and suck sap; their wings overlap at the tip, often forming an X or triangle pattern on the back.

children.topic: Read the damage, not just the insect
children.note: Round shot-holes in leaves suggest flea beetles, tunnels in corms or roots point to weevil grubs, small holes with powder in stored beans mean bruchids, and blackened or 'zebra' coffee beans suggest Antestia.
Many weevils hide in corms, roots, berries or seeds. Cutting open a few damaged parts and finding grubs is the surest confirmation.
Hypothenemus hampei is a tiny bark beetle native to Africa and now in almost every coffee country; it is generally rated the most damaging insect pest of coffee worldwide.
A dark brown to black beetle about the size of a pinhead (females roughly 2 mm). Only females fly; the smaller males stay inside the berry where they were born.

manas.q: Which sex of the coffee berry borer flies and leaves the berry?

children.note: The female bores into the berry, usually through the tip (the old flower end), and lays eggs in the bean. Larvae eat the seed and siblings mate inside, so one berry can produce a whole new brood.
A small round hole at the tip of green or ripe berries, sometimes with fine dust; inside, the beans have tunnels and grubs. Results are weight loss, fallen young berries and a poor cup grade.

manas.q: Where on the coffee berry do you look for the borer's entry hole?

children.note: Infested berries left on the bush after harvest or dropped on the ground keep the beetle alive between seasons; one study in Hawai'i quantified large post-harvest populations in these old 'raisin' berries.
It thrives in warmer, lower-altitude coffee, with long or overlapping flowering seasons that keep berries available all year. Climate warming is pushing it to higher farms.
Sample berries from a set number of trees regularly and count the share with holes; also watch catches in alcohol-baited traps after harvest, when females fly to find new berries.
Sanitation is the backbone, supported by traps, a fungus and natural enemies; Latin American IPM programmes combine all of these.
Strip off every ripe, overripe and dry berry at the end of harvest and pick up fallen berries from the ground; destroy them (boil, bury deeply or burn) so beetles cannot emerge.

manas.q: What is the single most important organic measure against coffee berry borer?

children.note: Simple funnel or bottle traps baited with a methanol–ethanol mix lure flying females, mainly after harvest. Traps reduce and monitor numbers but do not replace sanitation; handle methanol with care, it is poisonous.
This insect-killing fungus infects females while they are still entering the berry, so spraying is timed when new attacks are seen. It needs shade and humidity and is compatible with organic rules.

manas.q: When is Beauveria most effective against the berry borer?

children.note: Tiny African wasps (for example Prorops nasuta and Phymastichus coffea) attack the borer and have been released in several Latin American countries as classical biological control.
Drying parchment or cherry quickly to safe storage moisture stops beetles from continuing to breed in stored coffee.

Persistent synthetic insecticides once used against the borer, such as endosulfan, are now banned in many countries and never allowed in organic coffee; leaving gleanings on the ground undoes all other work.
Cosmopolites sordidus, the banana root borer, is a major pest of banana and plantain across the tropics, including East Africa's highland bananas.
A black, hard-bodied weevil around 1 cm long that hides by day in leaf sheaths and trash and moves at night. Adults are long-lived and rarely fly, so they spread mostly with planting material.

manas.q: How does the banana weevil mainly spread to new fields?

children.note: Grubs tunnel through the corm, leaving dark galleries when it is cut. Plants yellow and wilt, bunches are small, suckers are weak and plants snap or topple in wind.

manas.q: What do you see when you cut a weevil-damaged banana corm?

children.note: Toppling and poor growth can also come from root nematodes or Fusarium wilt; cut the corm and roots to check for weevil tunnels, nematode lesions or a red-brown vascular ring.
Use tissue-culture plantlets or suckers from clean fields. Pare away the outer corm tissue and discard suckers with tunnels; hot-water treatment of pared suckers is also used to clean them.
Split old pseudostem pieces laid cut-side down near the mat, or cut stumps (disc-on-stump), attract adults overnight; check every few days and kill the weevils collected.

manas.q: How is a banana pseudostem trap made and used?

children.note: After harvest, cut pseudostems low and chop them so they dry, removing breeding sites; keep the mat clear of rotting trash but use mulch away from the base.
Beauveria bassiana or Metarhizium can be dusted on pseudostem traps so visiting weevils pick up spores and carry infection back into the field. Fungal volatiles may also repel the weevil.
In the French Caribbean the insecticide chlordecone, used against banana weevil until 1993, still contaminates soil, water and food decades later, a strong reason to prevent this pest culturally.

manas.q: Which banned banana weevil insecticide still pollutes the French Caribbean?

children.note: Cylas formicarius is the most serious sweet potato pest worldwide; in Africa, C. puncticollis and C. brunneus also cause heavy losses.
Slender, ant-like weevils with long legs; C. formicarius has a metallic blue head and wing cases with a reddish middle. Larvae are white legless grubs inside vines and roots.

manas.q: What does an adult sweet potato weevil resemble?

children.note: Tunnels with dark frass inside storage roots and the vine base, cracked swollen stems and holes in roots. Even light damage makes roots bitter and unfit to eat because the plant produces defensive compounds.

manas.q: Why can lightly weevil-damaged sweet potatoes be inedible?

children.note: In dry weather soil cracks open and adult females walk down to exposed roots to lay eggs, so damage jumps in long dry spells and in late harvests.
Take planting cuttings from the top 20–30 cm of vines, which are rarely infested, and from fields without weevil damage.
Earth up the ridges and refill soil cracks during the season so roots stay covered and weevils cannot reach them.

manas.q: What field practice keeps sweet potato roots out of reach of weevils?

children.note: Rotate away from sweet potato, remove volunteer plants and old roots and vines after harvest, and avoid planting next to infested fields.
Harvest as soon as roots are mature rather than storing them in the ground for months; piecemeal harvesting over a long period gives weevils time to build up.
A synthetic female sex pheromone catches male C. formicarius in large numbers for monitoring and mass trapping, a method already used successfully in several countries.
Small leaf beetles (Chrysomelidae) that jump like fleas when disturbed. Phyllotreta species attack brassicas, Epitrix attack potato, tomato and eggplant, and Podagrica attack okra in Africa.
Many small round 'shot-holes' in leaves, worst on young seedlings, which can be killed or stunted in hot dry weather. Older plants usually tolerate the damage.

manas.q: What leaf symptom is typical of flea beetles?

children.note: Cover seedbeds and young crops with fine mesh immediately after sowing or transplanting; seal the edges with soil.
A border of a more attractive brassica (for example Chinese cabbage or mustard) draws flea beetles away from the main crop, where they can be controlled.
Transplant sturdy seedlings, water and mulch them so they outgrow early damage, and remove weedy relatives that host the beetles.
Yellow or white sticky cards catch adults; neem and kaolin clay can deter feeding, while spinosad and pyrethrins are organic-allowed options for heavy attacks.
Leaf-chewing beetles that strip foliage. The Colorado potato beetle is the best known; in the tropics, related leaf and ladybird beetles do similar damage.

Leptinotarsa decemlineata: yellow beetle with black stripes; larvae are red-orange humped grubs. A major pest in North America, Europe and parts of Asia, it is treated as a quarantine pest where absent.

manas.q: Which potato pest is a yellow beetle with black stripes?

children.note: In Africa and India, the red pumpkin beetle (Aulacophora) chews cucurbit leaves and Epilachna 'ladybird' beetles skeletonise leaves of eggplant, potato and cucurbits.
On small plots, shake beetles into a tin of soapy water and crush the bright yellow-orange egg clusters on leaf undersides.
Moving potatoes far from last season's field delays beetle arrival because adults overwinter in the soil; straw mulch also helps some predators.

A beetle-active strain of Bacillus thuringiensis (var. tenebrionis) kills young larvae; spinosad and Beauveria are also organic-allowed. The beetle is famous for resisting many synthetic insecticides.

manas.q: Which Bt variety targets leaf beetle larvae?

children.note: Meloidae such as Mylabris and Epicauta. Adults chew flowers and pods of beans, cowpea, pigeon pea and ornamentals; their larvae are actually useful predators of grasshopper eggs.
Their body fluid contains cantharidin, which raises painful blisters on skin; never crush them by hand and keep them out of animal feed.

manas.q: Why should blister beetles never be crushed by hand?

children.note: Large, brightly coloured beetles in groups eating flowers, so pods fail to form; damage is often patchy and short-lived.
Wear gloves and sweep or shake beetles into a bucket of soapy water early in the morning; protect high-value plots with netting during flowering.
Small seed beetles that breed inside dry pulses: Acanthoscelides obtectus and Zabrotes subfasciatus in common bean, Callosobruchus species in cowpea, green gram and other pulses.
Some species, such as A. obtectus, lay eggs on drying pods in the field, so infestation begins before harvest and explodes in store.
Round exit holes with little 'windows', white eggs glued on seeds, powder in the bag and adults flying from stored grain. Damaged seed loses weight, value and germination.

manas.q: What are the signs of bruchids in stored beans?

children.note: Harvest promptly when pods are dry, thresh and sun-dry the grain thoroughly, and sort out holed seeds before storage.
Airtight bags or containers starve bruchids of oxygen so they stop feeding and die; this chemical-free method is widely promoted for cowpea and beans.

manas.q: How does hermetic storage kill bruchids?

children.note: Coating seed with a little vegetable oil, mixing with ash or fine sand, and solarising grain in the sun all reduce attack; keep stores clean between seasons.
Synthetic storage fumigants and dusts are not allowed in organic produce and are dangerous in homes; never store new grain in old infested sacks.
Antestia bugs (Antestiopsis species) are shield bugs, not beetles, but rank among the worst pests of Arabica coffee in the East African highlands.
A shield-shaped stink bug with a dark body and orange and white markings. Nymphs and adults suck sap from buds, flowers, green berries and shoot tips.

manas.q: Is the Antestia bug a beetle?

children.note: Unlike many coffee pests, A. thunbergii increases with elevation, which models link to its temperature needs.
Blackened flower buds, rotten or 'zebra'-striped beans, berry drop and bushy fan-branching at shoot tips.

manas.q: Name two signs of Antestia damage in coffee.

children.note: Antestia feeding is associated with the 'potato taste' defect of East African coffee, which ruins the cup.
Count bugs on a sample of trees, for example by shaking branches over a sheet or using a light knockdown spray, and follow the local extension threshold before treating.
Prune and handle suckers to open the canopy, hand-pick bugs, encourage egg parasitoids and ants, and if counts are high use natural pyrethrins or Beauveria, both allowed in organic coffee.
Practices that work against most beetles and weevils at once.
Insect-killing fungi that infect through the insect's skin, so they work on chewing beetles that do not eat sprayed leaves. They need humidity and must not be mixed with fungicides.

manas.q: Why are insect-killing fungi useful against beetles?

children.note: Many weevils travel in suckers, cuttings and seed; starting clean is cheaper than any later control.
Rotating crops breaks the life cycle of soil-dwelling grubs and slow-moving adults that cannot follow the crop to a distant field.

manas.q: Which beetle pests are most affected by crop rotation?

children.note: Sex or aggregation pheromones and food lures (such as alcohols for berry borer) are used to monitor numbers, time interventions and mass-trap some species.
Removing fallen berries, crop residues and breeding sites, plus simple traps, reduces the next generation before it starts.

Botanicals like neem and pyrethrins, spinosad, Bt, kaolin and microbial fungi are generally allowed under organic rules; synthetic insecticides such as pyrethroids, organophosphates and neonicotinoids are not.

manas.q: Name two organic-allowed products for beetle control.

children.note: Short videos from extension services, universities and Access Agriculture.
A Hawai'i farm education video on sanitation, trapping and Beauveria for berry borer.
Access Agriculture summary of cleaning suckers, traps and sanitation against banana weevil.
Kerala Agricultural University shows how to make pseudostem traps (Malayalam).
LSU AgCenter explains integrated management of sweet potato weevil.
Utah State University Extension on identifying and managing flea beetles.
Purdue University on hermetic storage protecting cowpea from bruchids in Africa.
Reviews and reference pages for deeper study.
Review of coffee berry borer invasion history and research priorities worldwide.
How sanitation, traps, Beauveria and parasitoids are combined against berry borer.
Review of stored-pulse protection against Callosobruchus, including hermetic and botanical methods.
Free East African farmer information on pests and organic control, including banana weevil, berry borer and bruchids.

nodeData.note: Tephritid fruit flies lay eggs inside fruit and vegetables, and their maggots rot the crop from within. The Oriental fruit fly has spread across Africa since 2003. Organic control works best when neighbours act together across a whole area.

children.note: True fruit flies belong to the family Tephritidae. They are different from the tiny vinegar flies (Drosophila) that gather around overripe fruit in the kitchen.
Housefly-sized or smaller, often yellow and brown, with patterned or banded wings that they flick or wave while walking on fruit.

manas.q: How do true fruit flies differ from vinegar flies?

children.note: The female's pointed ovipositor pierces the fruit skin and places eggs beneath it, which is why damage starts invisibly.
Many species attack dozens of crops, breed fast in warm weather and adults fly between farms, so one neglected orchard can feed flies for a whole district.
A handful of species cause most losses in Africa, Asia and around the Mediterranean.
Bactrocera dorsalis: an Asian species and one of the world's most destructive fruit pests, attacking mango, citrus, guava, avocado, papaya, banana and many others.

manas.q: What is the scientific name of the Oriental fruit fly?

children.note: First found in Kenya in 2003 and described as 'Bactrocera invadens', it spread rapidly across sub-Saharan Africa; in 2015 it was shown to be the same species as B. dorsalis.

manas.q: In which year and country was the Oriental fruit fly first detected in Africa?

children.note: Ceratitis capitata (medfly), African in origin and now found on most continents, attacks citrus, stone fruit, coffee cherries and many other fruits.
Ceratitis rosa, the Natal fruit fly, prefers cooler, moister places than medfly; Ceratitis cosyra is a native African pest of mango and marula.
Zeugodacus cucurbitae (formerly Bactrocera cucurbitae) attacks cucumbers, melons, pumpkins, gourds and other cucurbits, often stinging flowers and very young fruit.

manas.q: Which fruit fly is the main pest of cucurbits?

children.note: In India, B. dorsalis is the main mango fruit fly, the peach fruit fly B. zonata hits guava and peach, and the melon fly is a key pest of gourds and melons.
Egg, maggot, pupa and adult; in warm weather a full generation can take only a few weeks, so populations climb quickly as fruit ripens.
The female lays a cluster of eggs just under the skin of ripening fruit; they hatch within a few days.
Creamy, legless maggots tunnel through the flesh for one to two weeks, while bacteria and fungi rot the fruit around them.
Grown maggots leave the fruit, often after it has fallen, and pupate a few centimetres deep in the soil under the tree.

manas.q: Where do fruit fly maggots pupate?

children.note: Adults need sugar and protein (from honeydew, bird droppings and bacteria) before laying eggs, and can live and lay for weeks to months.

manas.q: Why are protein baits attractive to female fruit flies?

children.note: Fallen fruit and the soil beneath trees are where the next generation is made, so sanitation and soil treatments cut it off at the source.
What the farmer sees on the tree, on the ground and in the crate.
Tiny puncture spots on the skin, sometimes with a drop of oozing sap or a dark halo around them; on mango and citrus they may be hard to see at first.

manas.q: What are the first signs of fruit fly attack on fruit?

children.note: Areas around the stings turn soft and watery and spread into larger rotten zones as maggots feed.
Infested fruit ripen unevenly and drop early; heaps of fallen fruit are a warning sign and a breeding ground.
Cut a suspect fruit: jumping cream-coloured maggots in the flesh confirm fruit flies.
Melon fly attacks cause young fruit to shrivel, deform or rot on the vine, and older fruit to rot from inside.
Anthracnose spots, mango seed weevil (which damages the seed, not the flesh) and false codling moth caterpillars in citrus can be confused with fruit fly damage.
Fruit flies cost farmers twice: through rotten fruit and through closed export markets.
Without control, losses in mango and other hosts can be very large; the Oriental fruit fly is ranked just behind medfly as the most important tephritid pest of fruit.
Importing countries treat B. dorsalis and many other non-native fruit flies as quarantine pests, so a single maggot found at the border can lead to rejected consignments or bans.

manas.q: Why can a single maggot stop a fruit export consignment?

children.note: When export or urban markets close, growers are left with low local prices and piles of spoilt fruit, which in turn breed more flies.
Traps show which species are present, when numbers rise and whether control is working. Count weekly and keep records.
A plant-derived lure strongly attractive to males of B. dorsalis and some related Bactrocera species; the standard tool for watching the Oriental fruit fly.

manas.q: Which lure attracts males of the Oriental fruit fly?

children.note: Attracts males of the melon fly and several other Bactrocera species; used in cucurbit fields.

manas.q: Which lure is used to monitor the melon fly?

children.note: Medfly males respond to trimedlure; other Ceratitis species such as the Natal and mango fruit flies are monitored with different lures, so use the right one for your target.
Protein-based food baits attract both sexes, especially females searching for protein, so they show egg-laying pressure better than male lures.
Catches are usually reported as flies per trap per day. Start monitoring before fruit set, refresh lures as the label says and act when counts begin to climb.
Fruit flies move between farms, so the best results come when all growers in an area combine several methods at the same time.
Collect fallen and infested fruit every few days throughout the season and destroy the maggots inside, removing the next generation before it pupates.

manas.q: Why must fallen fruit be collected every few days?

children.note: A screened tent where collected fruit is dumped: emerging flies are trapped inside, while the tiny parasitoid wasps that developed in the maggots escape through the mesh and return to the orchard.

manas.q: What does an augmentorium let out, and what does it keep in?

children.note: If no augmentorium is available, bury fruit deep enough that flies cannot emerge, or seal it in black plastic bags in the sun until the maggots die.

A protein food bait mixed with spinosad is sprayed in small spots on foliage, not over the fruit; females feed and die. Spinosad baits are allowed in EU and US organic rules, but check your certifier.

manas.q: How is a fruit fly food bait applied in organic orchards?

children.note: Blocks or stations with a male lure plus a killing agent remove so many males that females stay unmated. In organic farms the killing agent must be an allowed one, never a synthetic insecticide.
Paper or fabric bags placed on young fruit stop females from laying eggs; practical for high-value mango, guava, bitter gourd and melons.
Pick fruit at the mature-green stage and harvest regularly, because over-ripe fruit left on the tree is the most attractive to flies.
A small wasp that lays its eggs inside fruit fly eggs; icipe imported and released it in Africa against the Oriental fruit fly.

manas.q: Which life stage of the fruit fly does Fopius arisanus attack?

children.note: African weaver ants (Oecophylla longinoda) patrol mango trees and disturb or kill fruit flies; they are promoted in West and East Africa and need trees linked by branches or ropes.
Spores of the fungus Metarhizium anisopliae applied to the soil under the canopy infect larvae and pupae and emerging adults, attacking the generation hidden in the ground.

manas.q: Where is Metarhizium applied against fruit flies, and why?

children.note: The International Centre of Insect Physiology and Ecology (icipe), Nairobi, developed and scaled up a fruit fly package for African mango growers.
Monitoring traps, orchard sanitation with the augmentorium, food bait spot sprays, male annihilation, Metarhizium soil treatment and release of parasitoids.

manas.q: Name four components of icipe's fruit fly IPM package.

children.note: In Meru, Kenya, mango growers using the package reported on average a 48% rise in net mango income and 19% lower fruit fly losses compared with the previous season.
The same study found that cheaper, easy combinations such as sanitation plus food baits gave some of the largest gains, so farmers need not use every component.
Exporters must prove fruit is free of quarantine fruit flies; rules come from the importing country.
Some regions are officially recognised as free of a pest or as having low prevalence after trapping surveys, which opens markets.
Combining field control, monitoring, careful harvest, packhouse inspection and traceability gives layered protection that many importers accept.
Hot water, vapour heat, cold or irradiation treatments are used to kill eggs and larvae in fruit for strict markets; India uses vapour heat and irradiation to send mangoes abroad.
The EU lists Bactrocera dorsalis among its priority plant pests, so fruit hosts entering the EU face strict requirements and border checks.

manas.q: How does the EU classify Bactrocera dorsalis?

children.note: In Kenya, KEPHIS inspects and certifies fresh produce exports; in India, export plant health certification is handled by the Plant Protection Quarantine and Storage directorate.
Common mistakes that keep fruit flies thriving.
Fruit left to rot under trees or tipped into a shallow pit becomes a fly factory.
Full-cover sprays with synthetic insecticides are not allowed in organic farming, leave residues that can block exports and kill the natural enemies that help control flies.
One clean farm surrounded by neglected trees will keep receiving flies; coordinate with neighbours, schools and roadside trees.

manas.q: Why does area-wide action matter for fruit flies?

children.note: Traps without sanitation and baiting only count flies; they rarely protect a crop on their own.
Videos from icipe, Access Agriculture and Biovision.

icipe demonstrates mixing and applying food bait spot sprays.
icipe explains trap-based monitoring of fruit fly numbers.
icipe on fungal biopesticides used against fruit flies.

Biovision short on protecting the mango harvest from fruit flies ecologically.

nodeData.note: Termites, white grubs, cutworms, wireworms, millipedes, mole crickets, slugs, snails and burrowing rodents that attack seed and roots. How to recognise them and control them with organic methods: biological agents, botanicals, field practices, traps and predators.

children.note: Soil pests are insects and other animals that live in the soil and feed on seeds, roots, stem bases or tubers. Most damage happens out of sight, so farmers often notice it only when plants wilt or fall over.
Because the attackers stay underground, the first signs are gaps in the stand, wilting on sunny days, stunted patches or plants that pull out easily. Digging is the only way to confirm the cause.

manas.q: What is the only sure way to confirm a soil pest problem?

children.topic: Not every soil animal is a pest
children.note: Termites, millipedes and beetle larvae also break down dead plant material and mix the soil. Most become crop pests only when other food is scarce or populations are unusually high.

Termites, white grubs, cutworms, wireworms, millipedes, mole crickets, slugs and snails, plus burrowing rodents such as mole rats. Root-knot and other plant-parasitic nematodes are covered in the nematode and disease maps.
Once roots are eaten there is no spray that brings them back. Organic control relies on soil preparation, crop timing, biological agents in the soil and monitoring before and at planting.

Social insects that live in colonies with a queen, workers and soldiers. In the tropics, including East Africa and India, they are among the most damaging pests of maize, groundnuts, sugarcane and young trees.

Mound builders such as Macrotermes raise large earth mounds; field (subterranean) termites such as Microtermes, Odontotermes and Ancistrotermes nest out of sight in the soil. Both forage widely through tunnels.

manas.q: Name two genera of crop-damaging termites in Africa or India.

children.note: Many crop-damaging termites farm a fungus (Termitomyces) inside the nest on chewed plant material, which they cannot fully digest alone. This is why they collect so much dry plant matter.

manas.q: What do fungus-growing termites grow inside their nests?

children.note: Termites hollow out roots and the lower stem, often late in the season. Plants lodge (fall over) near maturity, cobs touch the ground and rot, and yield is lost. Damage is worst in dry spells and on drought-stressed plants.

manas.q: When in the season do termites usually make maize lodge?

children.note: Newly transplanted tree seedlings (eucalyptus, grevillea, fruit trees) can be ring-barked or have their taproot eaten, then wilt and die suddenly. Older healthy trees usually tolerate them.
In groundnut, termites scar and bore into pods and the taproot, which also lets in moulds and raises aflatoxin risk. Sugarcane setts, wheat and vegetables can be hit too.
Soil sheeting or mud tunnels on stems and stakes, hollow stems packed with soil, wilting plants that pull out easily, and workers found when the base of the plant is dug up.

manas.q: What do termite mud sheets on a stem look like and mean?

children.note: Drought stress, sandy soils low in organic matter, bare soil with no crop residues left for termites to eat, and fields recently cleared from bush or grassland.
Their tunnels let rain soak in and their mounds concentrate nutrients; in dryland Africa they rebuild degraded soils. Aim to protect crops, not to wipe termites out.

White grubs are the larvae of chafer beetles (scarabs), for example Phyllophaga in the Americas, Holotrichia in India and Schizonycha in Africa. They chew roots of maize, potatoes, beans, sugarcane and pasture.
Fat, soft, cream-white larvae with a brown head and three pairs of legs, lying curled in a C shape in the soil. Large ones can reach 3–4 cm.

manas.q: In what shape does a white grub lie in the soil?

children.note: Adult beetles fly out at the first good rains, mate and lay eggs in soil. Most species have one generation a year (some take two or three); the larger grubs do the most damage.
Roots are pruned away, so plants wilt, yellow and are stunted in patches, and can be lifted with no roots. Birds digging in a field are often a clue.
Female beetles prefer to lay eggs in moist soil rich in fresh organic matter. Uncomposted manure can raise grub numbers; well-made compost does not have this effect.

manas.q: Why does raw manure tend to increase white grubs?

children.note: Many chafer species are attracted to light at night. Community light traps at the first rains catch egg-laying females; in India this is part of standard white-grub management.
Caterpillars of night-flying moths, mostly Agrotis species (A. ipsilon, A. segetum). They hide in the soil by day and feed at night.
Young seedlings of maize, cabbage, tomato, tobacco and beans are cut through at or just below soil level, so the plant falls over overnight. Several plants in a row can be lost to one larva.

manas.q: What is the typical sign of cutworm damage on seedlings?

children.note: At dawn, dig gently around a freshly cut plant: a greasy grey-brown caterpillar that curls up when touched is usually within a few centimetres.
Moths lay eggs on weeds and crop residues. Clearing weeds two to three weeks before planting removes egg sites and starves young larvae before the crop emerges.
A ring of paper, cardboard or a cut plastic bottle pushed into the soil around each transplant stops larvae reaching the stem. Practical for vegetable beds, not for large fields.
Larvae of click beetles (family Elateridae). They live in soil for several years and attack potatoes, maize, cereals and root crops.
Slender, hard, shiny, yellow-brown larvae 1–3 cm long, unlike soft white grubs. Adults are the beetles that flip in the air with a click.
They bore narrow round holes into potato tubers and eat germinating seed, causing gaps. Damage is highest in the first years after grassland or long fallow is ploughed.

manas.q: After which land use are wireworm problems usually worst?

children.note: Bury a handful of soaked maize or wheat seed, or a cut potato, 10 cm deep and mark it. Dig it up after about a week and count larvae to judge the risk before planting potatoes.
Long, many-legged animals that mostly eat decaying plant matter. They become pests in some seasons, especially in Africa and India.
In dry spells or where heavy mulch is next to young plants, they feed on germinating seed, seedlings and groundnut pods. Damage is usually patchy.
Keep thick mulch a little away from emerging seedlings, plant into moist soil for fast emergence and encourage poultry and birds. Wood ash rings are a traditional deterrent with little test data.
Brown, velvety crickets (Gryllotalpa, Neoscapteriscus) with spade-like front legs that tunnel near the surface.
Tunnelling lifts and dries out seedbeds and nurseries, and they bite off roots and stems of seedlings. Lawns, rice nurseries and vegetable beds are often hit.
In Florida, a parasitic wasp (Larra), a parasitic fly (Ormia) and an insect-killing nematode (Steinernema scapterisci) were introduced and brought pest mole crickets down over years.

manas.q: Which three natural enemies were used against mole crickets in Florida?

children.note: Pouring a bucket of water with a little soap over a square metre drives mole crickets to the surface within minutes, a simple way to see how many there are.
Molluscs that rasp holes in seedlings, leaves and tubers, mainly in cool, damp weather and under heavy mulch or weeds.
Ragged holes in leaves, seedlings eaten to the stalk overnight and shiny slime trails. Go out with a torch after dark to see them feeding.

manas.q: What shiny sign shows that slugs or snails have been feeding?

children.note: Lissachatina (Achatina) fulica is a big invasive snail in Kenya, India and many tropical islands. It eats many crops and should be hand-collected and destroyed; it can carry a rat lungworm, so wear gloves.
Boards, upturned pots or cabbage leaves give them a daytime hiding place; check and collect each morning. Shallow traps of beer or yeast water also draw slugs in.
Ferric phosphate slug pellets are permitted in organic farming in many standards and break down to iron and phosphate in soil. Metaldehyde pellets are not allowed in organic.

manas.q: Which type of slug pellet is accepted in organic farming?

children.note: Burrowing rodents eat seed, roots and tubers. In East Africa mole rats (Tachyoryctes) and field rats are common.
Fresh soil mounds without an open hole (mole rats), rows of dug-up seed, gnawed tubers and wilting plants with roots chewed off.
Traps set in the runs, clean field edges with short grass, perches and nest boxes for owls and hawks, and cats or dogs around stores. Poison baits are not allowed under organic standards.
Count soil pests before planting so you know whether action is needed. Exact thresholds depend on crop and region, so use them as a guide only.
Dig several pits about 30 × 30 cm and 20–30 cm deep across the field, sieve or break the soil and count grubs, cutworms and wireworms. Record the numbers each season.

manas.q: How big is a typical soil sampling pit for counting grubs?

children.note: Cutworms, slugs and mole crickets are active at night. A short walk at first light finds fresh damage and the pests before they hide.
Soil pests are patchy. Marking damaged spots shows where to treat next season instead of the whole field.
Insect-killing fungi and nematodes live naturally in soil and can be added as products. They act slowly and need moisture, but suit organic systems well.

Metarhizium anisopliae and related species are green-spored soil fungi that infect insects through the skin. They are among the best-tested biological agents against white grubs, wireworms and some termites.

manas.q: How does Metarhizium get into an insect?

children.note: Beauveria bassiana is a white-spored relative used mainly against insects above ground, but also against some soil beetles and weevils. It needs humid conditions to sporulate.
Mix spore powder with well-made compost or FYM and apply in the planting furrow or planting hole, then water. Keep away from chemical fungicides and strong sun, and repeat each season.
Both fungi can live in crop roots as harmless endophytes after a soil drench, which may give longer-lasting protection. Field benefit varies and is still being studied.
Termites groom and isolate infected nestmates, so fungal spores rarely destroy a whole colony. Fungi are best seen as part of termite management, not a cure.

manas.q: Why do insect-killing fungi rarely wipe out termite colonies?

children.note: Microscopic worms (Steinernema, Heterorhabditis) that enter grubs, cutworms and weevil larvae and release bacteria that kill the host in a few days. They then multiply inside and spread to new hosts.

manas.q: Which two nematode genera are used to kill soil insects?

children.note: Apply in the evening or on cloudy days to moist soil, water in, and keep moist for two weeks. They die in sun, heat and dry soil, and must be used before the expiry date.
Plant-based materials worked into soil can deter or slow soil pests. Effects are usually partial and depend on dose and soil life.

The residue left after pressing neem seed for oil. Mixed into soil at planting it acts as an organic fertiliser and its limonoids (such as azadirachtin) deter and disrupt grubs, termites and nematodes. Widely used in India.

manas.q: What is neem cake and how does it act against soil pests?

children.note: A traditional dusting around seedlings against cutworms, termites and slugs. Fresh ash is caustic and drying, but it washes out with rain, raises soil pH, and good trial evidence is scarce. Use small amounts only.

manas.q: What are two drawbacks of wood ash as a pest treatment?

children.note: Leaves of Tithonia, Tephrosia, castor or Lantana are traditionally added to planting holes against termites. Most evidence is from farmer experience and small trials, so test on a small area first.
Field practices are the base of organic soil-pest control, but each has costs as well as benefits.

Ploughing in the dry season brings grubs and pupae to the surface where sun and birds kill them. But frequent deep tillage harms earthworms, soil structure and organic matter, so use it as a targeted tool, not every year.

manas.q: What is the trade-off of ploughing to expose white grubs?

children.note: Flooding a field for a few days drowns cutworms, mole crickets and grubs, and is natural in paddy rice. In rain-fed farming it is rarely possible, and it can damage soil structure.
Mulch gives termites something to eat besides the crop and builds soil, but it also shelters slugs, snails and millipedes. Keep mulch on the field but pull it back a hand-width from young stems.

manas.q: Why can mulch reduce termite attack on the crop itself?

children.note: Rotating away from grass, cereals and potatoes for a year or two, for example into legumes or brassicas, breaks the food supply of grubs and wireworms.
Timely planting, good soil moisture and balanced nutrition help plants outgrow root damage. Termite damage to maize is clearly worse in drought-stressed fields.
Apply manure only after it is fully composted. Hot composting also kills grub and cutworm stages that may be in the heap.
Natural predators and simple traps keep soil pest numbers down at low cost.
Egrets, crows, hornbills and starlings follow ploughing and eat grubs and cutworms. Perches and trees on field edges help them stay.
Chickens let onto a field after harvest or before planting scratch out grubs and cutworms; ducks are very good at eating slugs and snails. Keep them off young crops.

manas.q: Which poultry is especially good at eating slugs and snails?

children.note: Ground beetles, rove beetles, centipedes and ants feed on soil pest eggs and larvae. Permanent grassy strips and reduced spraying keep them in the field.
Moist bran mixed with a little molasses and spread at dusk draws cutworms out; they can be collected at night. Commercial Bt or nematode baits use the same idea.
Traditional East African practice often targets the mound and its queen rather than the termites in the field.

Digging out a Macrotermes mound and removing the queen can stop that colony, and farmers in Kenya and Uganda do this. It is heavy work, colonies of some species can re-queen, and other colonies nearby keep foraging.

manas.q: What are two limits of removing the termite queen?

children.note: Mound soil is richer in clay and nutrients and is used for bricks and as fertiliser. Removing only mounds close to young trees and high-value crops keeps the benefits.
Plant seedlings with compost, water well, mulch with dry grass away from the stem, and avoid planting into wood debris. Healthy, unstressed seedlings are attacked less.
Some common practices are illegal in organic farming or harmful to people and soil.
Chlorpyrifos, fipronil, imidacloprid and similar soil insecticides and seed dressings are not allowed in organic certification, and many are banned or restricted in Kenya, India and the EU.

manas.q: Are imidacloprid seed dressings allowed in organic farming?

children.note: Pouring used engine oil, kerosene or diesel into mounds or planting holes poisons soil and water and is never organic.
Dig before acting. Earthworms, beetles and many termites in a healthy soil are helpers, and killing them hurts soil fertility.
Short videos from research, extension and farmer-to-farmer channels.
Kenya’s Agroecology Hub — farmers in western Kenya show how they cut termite damage without chemicals.
University of Wisconsin IPM — identifying grubs, wireworms, seedcorn maggot and cutworms early in the season.
Virginia Tech Eastern Shore AREC — wireworm biology and management in potatoes.
University of Florida entomology — the fly, the wasp and the nematode used against mole crickets.
An experienced gardener shows a simple pot trap for slugs and snails.
Reliable starting points for deeper study.

nodeData.note: Insects, moulds and aflatoxin that attack grain and beans after harvest, and the organic ways to stop them: harvest and drying, airtight storage, inert dusts, botanicals, clean stores and monitoring.

children.note: After months of work in the field, a large share of grain can be lost in the store to insects, moulds and rodents. Good storage protects food, income and health.
A major review reports that cereal losses in storage can reach 50–60% where storage is poor, and that improved storage methods can cut losses to as little as 1–2%.

manas.q: How low can improved storage bring cereal storage losses?

children.note: Insect damage lowers weight, germination and market price, and holes made by insects let moulds in, raising the risk of aflatoxin.
Organic standards do not allow synthetic storage insecticides or chemical fumigants, so the system relies on drying, cleaning, airtight storage, inert dusts and botanicals.

manas.q: What does organic grain storage rely on instead of synthetic insecticides?

children.note: Sitophilus zeamais (maize weevil) and S. oryzae (rice weevil) are the most widespread storage pests of maize, sorghum, rice and wheat in the tropics.
Small dark-brown beetles, about 3–4 mm long, with a long snout and often four faint orange spots on the wing cases. The two species look almost the same.

manas.q: What body feature identifies a weevil?

children.note: The female chews a hole, lays one egg inside the kernel and seals it. The larva eats and pupates inside, so infested grain looks clean until adults emerge.
Neat round exit holes in kernels, fine flour dust, grain that feels warm, and kernels that float in water because they are hollow.

manas.q: Why do weevil-infested kernels float in water?

children.note: Weevils fly from old stores to maturing maize in the field, especially where husk cover is poor. Late harvest gives them more time to settle in.
Prostephanus truncatus, a small bostrichid beetle native to Mexico and Central America, is the most destructive pest of farm-stored maize and dried cassava in East and West Africa.
It was accidentally introduced to Tanzania in the late 1970s and spread through much of sub-Saharan Africa, including Kenya. Models show it could still spread to new areas.

manas.q: Where did the larger grain borer first arrive in Africa?

children.note: A cylindrical dark-brown beetle about 3–4 mm long whose head is tucked under the thorax, so no snout is visible from above. It is a borer, not a weevil.
Adults tunnel from grain to grain and leave large piles of fine grain dust. They also bore into dried cassava chips, wooden store beams and sacks, and can destroy cob maize in a few months.

manas.q: What does LGB leave behind that weevils usually do not?

children.topic: Store shelled, not on the cob
children.note: LGB does best on maize kept on the cob, especially with husks. Shelling, drying well and storing in airtight containers greatly reduces damage.

A small predatory beetle from Central America, Teretrius nigrescens, was released in several African countries from the 1990s and feeds on LGB in the wild. It lowers outbreaks but does not protect a single store on its own.
Traps baited with the LGB aggregation pheromone show when beetles are flying in an area, so farmers know when to harvest promptly and seal stores.
Bruchids (bean weevils) such as Acanthoscelides obtectus on common beans and Callosobruchus maculatus and C. chinensis on cowpea, grams and pigeon pea.
Small round "windows" on seeds where larvae inside are close to the surface, then neat exit holes, powder and small oval beetles running in the store.

manas.q: What are the round "windows" on stored beans?

children.note: Eggs are often laid on drying pods before harvest, so newly harvested beans can already be infested. Fast harvest and threshing help.
Mixing beans or cowpeas with a small amount of vegetable oil coats the seed so eggs and young larvae suffocate. This is a long-standing household method for seed and food beans.
Moth larvae feed on grain and flour, mainly in the top layer of a store.
Sitotroga cerealella. Larvae develop inside maize, rice, sorghum and wheat kernels; adults leave small round holes, often with a thin flap. Infestation can begin in the field.

manas.q: Which storage moth develops inside whole kernels?

children.note: Plodia interpunctella. Larvae spin silk webbing through flour, broken grain, dried fruit and nuts. A pest of processed food in homes and shops worldwide.

manas.q: What sign typically shows Indian meal moth?

children.note: Most moth damage is in the upper 30 cm of grain in bulk. Airtight containers, fine-mesh covers and stirring the top layer limit them.
Several more beetles attack stored grain and flour.

children.topic: Flour beetles and lesser grain borer
children.note: Red flour beetle (Tribolium castaneum) feeds on broken grain and flour; lesser grain borer (Rhyzopertha dominica) bores whole grains like a small LGB. Both follow primary pests.
Trogoderma granarium hairy larvae devastate grain in hot, dry regions including India. Many countries list it as a quarantine pest, so report suspected finds.
Moulds such as Aspergillus, Fusarium and Penicillium grow on damp or damaged grain. Some produce mycotoxins; aflatoxins are the most dangerous.
A group of poisons made mainly by Aspergillus flavus and A. parasiticus on maize, groundnuts, sorghum and other crops. Aflatoxin B1 is the most potent.

manas.q: Which two fungi mainly produce aflatoxins?

children.note: High doses cause acute liver failure (aflatoxicosis); long-term low exposure is linked to liver cancer and weakened immunity. Animals fed contaminated feed grow poorly and dairy cows pass a form (M1) into milk.
In 2004 one of the largest known aflatoxicosis outbreaks hit eastern and central Kenya, with 317 cases and 125 deaths, traced to contaminated home-grown maize.

manas.q: How many deaths did Kenya’s 2004 aflatoxin outbreak cause?

children.note: Kenya has had repeated outbreaks, especially in the drier eastern counties such as Makueni and Kitui, where a toxic strain type of A. flavus is common.
Aflatoxin has no colour, smell or taste in grain, and normal cooking does not destroy it. Visible mould is a warning, but clean-looking grain can still be contaminated.

manas.q: Does cooking destroy aflatoxin?

children.note: Drought and heat stress during grain fill, insect damage, late harvest, drying on bare ground, rain on harvested crop and storage above safe moisture.
Rapid test kits and labs measure aflatoxin in parts per billion. Buyers, millers and feed makers in Kenya increasingly test lots, and contaminated grain must not be sold for food or feed.
Aflasafe products use native strains of Aspergillus flavus that cannot make aflatoxin to crowd out the toxic strains in the field.

The non-toxic strains are coated on sterile sorghum grain and spread on the soil before the crop flowers. They grow, sporulate and take over the niche on the crop, leaving less room for toxin-producing strains.

manas.q: How do atoxigenic A. flavus strains reduce aflatoxin?

children.note: Reviews of African trials report that atoxigenic biocontrol reduces aflatoxin in maize and groundnut by about 70–90%.

manas.q: By how much does atoxigenic biocontrol typically cut aflatoxin?

children.note: Each product is made from strains native to that country. Versions have been registered in Kenya, Nigeria, Senegal and The Gambia, among others; the Kenyan one was developed with KALRO.
It works in the field, not in a store: grain must still be dried and stored well. Organic farmers should confirm with their certifier whether a given product is permitted.
Most storage problems are decided at harvest. Dry, clean, undamaged grain stores well; damp grain spoils whatever the container.
Harvest as soon as the crop is mature and dry enough. Leaving maize in the field for weeks invites weevils, LGB, moulds and termites.
Dry cobs or grain on tarpaulins, mats, raised cribs or cement floors, not on the ground, where soil carries Aspergillus spores and moisture.

manas.q: Why should grain never be dried on bare soil?

children.note: Grain should be dried to about 13% moisture before storage to keep insects and moulds slow. Moisture meters give a reading; simpler tests give a yes/no.

manas.q: To about what moisture should grain be dried before storage?

children.note: Shake a little dry salt with grain in a clean, dry glass bottle for a few minutes. If salt sticks to the glass, the grain is still too wet to store.

manas.q: What does it mean if salt sticks to the bottle in the salt test?

children.note: Remove mouldy, shrivelled, broken and insect-damaged cobs and kernels; they carry most of the aflatoxin and insects. Feed them to nobody.
Hermetic (airtight) storage starves insects of oxygen without chemicals. PICS bags, developed at Purdue University, are the best-known type in Africa and Asia.
Inside a sealed bag, insects and grain use up oxygen and build up carbon dioxide. Insects stop feeding, stop breeding and die, so damage stays very low.

manas.q: What kills insects inside a hermetic bag?

children.note: Two inner liners of thick polyethylene sit inside an outer woven polypropylene bag. Each liner is twisted, folded and tied separately to make the seal airtight.

manas.q: How many layers does a PICS bag have?

children.note: Airtight bags hold moisture in. Grain stored too damp can still go mouldy, and opening bags often lets oxygen back in and raises fungal growth and aflatoxin risk.

links.label: 📄 J Stored Prod Res 2016 (opening PICS bags)

children.note: A survey of 613 farmers in eastern Kenya found hermetic storage use rose from about 54% in 2015 to 91% in 2017, with PICS the most used and storage judged profitable.
Store bags off the floor, away from rats and sharp objects, and check liners for holes before reuse. A hole as small as a pin lets air in and the seal fails.
Airtight galvanised-steel silos built by trained local artisans, promoted by CIMMYT and others for farm households in Africa and Central America.
When sealed, a silo is hermetic like a PICS bag and also keeps out rats and birds. Sizes range from a few hundred kilograms to a few tonnes.
Before sealing, a lit candle placed on top of the grain burns off part of the oxygen; it goes out when oxygen is low. The lid is then sealed with rubber or grease.

manas.q: Why do farmers put a burning candle in a metal silo before sealing?

children.note: They cost more than bags at the start but can last many years, so cost per year is often low. Keep them in the shade to avoid heating and condensation.
Dusts that kill insects physically, not chemically. Many are permitted in organic storage.
A fine powder of fossil algae shells. It scratches and absorbs the waxy outer layer of insects, so they lose water and die. Grain is usually treated at low rates of around 1 g per kg.

manas.q: How does diatomaceous earth kill stored-grain insects?

children.note: DE kills faster at higher temperature and lower humidity, so it suits dry grain in warm stores. In very humid conditions it works more slowly.

links.label: 📄 J Econ Entomol 2000 (DE vs temperature & RH)

children.note: A traditional method: mixing clean, sieved wood ash or fine sand with grain fills the spaces between kernels and hinders insects. It works best in small, full containers.
Wear a dust mask when mixing; use food-grade amorphous DE, not the crystalline pool-filter type. Sieve or wash grain before milling.
Plant materials mixed with grain or used to line stores repel or kill storage insects. Results are usually partial and fade with time.
Dried neem leaves or neem seed powder mixed with grain or seed deter weevils and bruchids. A long-standing practice in India and East Africa.

manas.q: Which tree’s leaves and seed powder are a traditional grain protectant?

children.note: Leaves of this "fish-bean" shrub are dried and mixed with stored beans and maize in East and Southern Africa. They contain rotenoids, which are toxic: use for seed or with care, and never near fish ponds.
Dried chilli or black pepper powder repels insects and is used with beans and grain in many homes. Taste and handling need care.
Lantana or eucalyptus leaves layered with stored maize are reported to discourage LGB and weevils, as part of a wider storage plan.
Purified rotenone is no longer permitted in EU organic farming. Check your certifier’s rules before using any botanical product beyond home use.
Most new infestations come from leftover grain and dirty stores.
Sweep out old grain, dust and husks, repair cracks and burn or bury the sweepings. Old stores can carry LGB and weevils waiting for new grain.

manas.q: Where do new storage infestations usually come from?

children.note: Dip used sacks in boiling water or sun them well before reuse to kill hidden eggs and larvae.
Stack bags on pallets off the floor and away from walls, keep new grain away from old, and keep the store cool, dry and rat-proof.
Check stored grain regularly so problems are caught early.
Take samples from the top, middle and sides, sieve and count insects, and look for dust, webbing, warmth, caking or a musty smell.
Hot spots, damp lumps or a sour, mouldy smell show moisture or insect activity. Spread, re-dry and sort the grain at once.
Pheromone traps catch LGB and moths; probe and pitfall traps show beetles in bulk grain. They warn early, before damage is visible.
Common shortcuts that are illegal in organic farming or dangerous.

children.topic: No synthetic grain dusts or fumigants
children.note: Synthetic insecticide dusts and phosphine fumigation tablets are not allowed under organic standards. Phosphine is also highly poisonous to people when misused in homes.

manas.q: Is phosphine fumigation allowed in organic storage?

children.note: Never mix mouldy grain with good grain to sell or feed it; the toxin remains and spreads to the whole lot.

Access Agriculture — how aflatoxin develops after harvest and how to prevent it.
