nodeData.note: Weeds are managed, not eradicated, on an organic farm. The aim is to stop them hurting yield during the crop's sensitive window and to shrink the weed seed bank year by year — using prevention, smart timing, soil cover, tools and living plants instead of synthetic herbicides.

children.note: Weeds compete with crops for light, water and nutrients, and some host pests and diseases. But they also bring real benefits, so the goal is control, not a bare field.
Weeds take water, nitrogen and light, especially when the crop is young. Losses are often bigger on poor, dry soils where every resource counts.

manas.q: What do weeds compete with crops for?

children.note: Some weeds carry viruses, nematodes or insects that move onto crops; e.g. nightshade-family weeds can host pests of tomato and potato.
They cover bare soil against erosion, feed pollinators and natural enemies with flowers, and can be cut for mulch, fodder or compost.

manas.q: Name three benefits weeds can give a farm.

children.note: Certain weeds hint at soil conditions — e.g. many sedges and rushes point to waterlogging; Striga thrives where soil fertility is low. Use them as clues, then confirm with a test.
In Kenya amaranth (terere) and African nightshade (managu) are valued leafy vegetables; in India many 'weeds' are eaten or used as fodder.
The store of live weed seeds and buds in the soil. Most weeds that appear each season come from this bank, so long-term success means stopping new seed being added.
Seeds shed in past seasons that lie dormant at different depths. Only a small share germinates each year; the rest can wait for years.

manas.q: What is the weed seed bank?

children.note: A few plants left to flower can refill the bank. The old saying is 'one year's seeding, seven years' weeding'.

manas.q: Why must weeds be removed before they set seed?

children.note: Turning soil brings buried seeds to the light and triggers a flush of germination. Shallow cultivation and less tillage expose fewer seeds.
Couch grass, nutsedge and similar weeds spread by rhizomes, tubers or runners. Chopping them with a rotavator can multiply them; exhaust them by repeated removal instead.
The window in the crop's life when weeds must be kept down to avoid yield loss. Weeds before or after it do much less harm.
Weeds that emerge with the crop and stay through the early weeks cut yield most; once the crop canopy closes, later weeds matter less.

manas.q: What is the critical period for weed control?

links.label: 📄 Source: Knezevic et al. 2002, Weed Science

children.note: Weed early and on time — usually the first weeks after emergence or transplanting; exact timing differs by crop, season and weed pressure.

links.label: 📄 Source: Knezevic et al. 2002, Weed Science

children.note: Transplanted vegetables and rice start ahead of the weeds, which makes early weeding easier than in direct-sown crops.
The cheapest weed is the one that never arrives. Stop seeds entering the field and give weeds no gap.
Buy certified or well-cleaned seed; weedy home-saved seed and seedlings spread weeds like Striga and dodder.

manas.q: Name two ways weed seeds arrive on a farm.

children.note: A compost heap that heats up well (around 55°C or more, turned) kills most weed seeds. Cold heaps and raw manure can spread them.
Wash ploughs, tractors and boots between fields, especially after working in Parthenium or Striga patches.
Prepare the bed, let rain or irrigation trigger a weed flush, kill it with a very shallow hoe or flame, then sow without stirring deeper soil.

manas.q: How does a stale seedbed work?

children.note: Cut or graze edges and bunds before weeds seed, while leaving some flowering strips for beneficial insects.
Covering the soil blocks light so weed seeds do not germinate, and also saves water and feeds soil life.
Straw, grass, crop residues, leaves or wood chips. A thick layer (several cm) is needed to suppress weeds; top it up as it rots.

manas.q: Why must an organic mulch be thick?

children.note: Hay or grass cut after seeding can sow new weeds. Use residues collected before flowering or composted material.
Generally allowed under organic standards if it is non-PVC (e.g. polyethylene) and fully removed after use. Never burn it or plough it in; check your standard for biodegradable films.

manas.q: What rules apply to plastic mulch in organic farming?

children.note: Black tarps laid on beds for some weeks kill emerging weeds (occultation). Clear plastic on moist soil in hot sun heats it enough to kill many seeds (solarisation).
Living plants that fill the gap so weeds cannot grow, while adding organic matter and often nitrogen.
They shade the soil, take up resources first, and some release chemicals from residues that slow weed germination.
Fast, dense crops such as buckwheat, cowpea, velvet bean (Mucuna) or sweet potato that close the canopy quickly and choke weeds.

manas.q: Give two examples of smother crops.

children.note: A thick cereal rye or rye-vetch cover is flattened with a roller-crimper and the cash crop planted through the mat — used on organic farms in temperate regions.
Mucuna, lablab, Desmodium and dolichos are used as cover and fodder legumes; they suppress weeds and fix nitrogen.
Growing two or more crops together closes the canopy sooner and leaves less space and light for weeds.
Maize with beans, cowpea or groundnut covers the ground better than maize alone, and the legume adds nitrogen.
A low legume grown between crop rows (e.g. Desmodium in maize) keeps weeds down all season.
Physical removal is the backbone of organic weed control. Tools work best on tiny weeds in dry, sunny weather.
Cheap and universal; a sharp, shallow cut is better than deep digging that brings up new seeds and damages crop roots.
Push-pull blades slice weeds just below the surface with little effort, ideal for vegetable beds.
A hoe blade on a wheel lets one person weed long rows standing up, much faster than a hand hoe.
Cono and rotary weeders are pushed between rice rows (as in SRI); they uproot weeds and churn them into the mud, also aerating the soil.

manas.q: What does a cono weeder do in rice?

children.note: Seedlings just germinated are killed by the lightest touch. A few minutes early saves hours later.

manas.q: When is the best time to hoe weeds?

children.note: Tine weeders, finger weeders and inter-row cultivators do the same job on larger farms.
Short bursts of heat burst weed cells; the plant wilts and dies within a day or two. Allowed in organic farming.
A gas burner passes quickly over the weeds — they are heated, not burnt to ash. Squeezing a leaf leaves a thumbprint if it worked.

manas.q: Does flame weeding need to burn weeds to ash?

children.note: Broadleaf seedlings at an early leaf stage; pre-emergence in slow crops like carrots and onions, just before the crop appears.
Grasses and perennials regrow from protected growing points. Keep fire risk in mind in dry residues and windy weather.
Steam and hot water are used on small areas and in greenhouses; solarisation uses the sun.
Animals can turn weeds into meat, milk or eggs.
Grazing in orchards, plantations and after harvest keeps weeds short; poultry also eat seeds and insects.
Keep stock off crops they damage, avoid toxic weeds (e.g. Lantana), and follow organic rules on manure near produce for fresh eating.
Some plants release chemicals from roots or residues that stop other plants germinating or growing.
Rye and sorghum residues and some brassicas can suppress small-seeded weeds for some weeks.

manas.q: What is allelopathy?

children.note: Desmodium root exudates cause Striga seeds to germinate and then block them from attaching to maize roots.

links.label: 📄 Source: Khan et al. 2014, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B

children.note: The same chemicals can slow small-seeded crops sown straight into the residues; leave a gap or transplant.
A parasitic weed that steals water and nutrients from cereal roots. In East Africa it is one of the biggest causes of maize and sorghum yield loss.
Striga hermonthica and S. asiatica attack maize, sorghum, millet, rice and sugarcane; S. gesnerioides attacks cowpea.

manas.q: Which crops does Striga hermonthica attack?

links.label: 📄 Source: Nzioki et al. 2016, Frontiers in Plant Science

children.note: Its tiny seeds germinate only when cereal roots release signals (strigolactones), then attach underground and drain the host before the weed even emerges.

links.label: 📄 Source: Cell 2025 — Striga resistance via lower strigolactone exudation

children.note: Stunted maize with wilting, yellowing or scorched-looking leaves, as if drought-stressed; later pink-purple flowered Striga plants appear around the stems.
Low soil fertility, continuous cereal cropping and huge, long-lived seed banks in the soil.
Maize intercropped with Desmodium and bordered by Napier or Brachiaria grass suppresses Striga, repels stemborers, adds nitrogen and produces fodder.

manas.q: Name the companion plants in push-pull.

links.label: 📄 Source: Khan et al. 2014, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B
📄 Source: Midega et al. 2018, Crop Protection

children.note: Resistant or tolerant maize and sorghum varieties support fewer Striga plants; combine them with push-pull and fertility building.

links.label: 📄 Source: Current progress in Striga management, Plant Physiology 2021

children.note: A Striga-specific fungus (Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. strigae) can be coated onto seed, e.g. via inoculated toothpicks; on-farm trials showed less Striga emergence.

links.label: 📄 Source: Nzioki et al. 2016, Frontiers in Plant Science

children.note: Rotate with legumes (soybean, groundnut, cotton act as trap crops), add manure or compost, and hand-pull Striga before it flowers.
Herbicide-coated imazapyr-resistant maize controls Striga but uses a synthetic herbicide, so it is not allowed in certified organic farming.
Leafless root parasites (Orobanche and Phelipanche) that attack tomato, faba bean, sunflower, tobacco and mustard.
Pale or purplish flowering spikes appear at the crop base after damage is done; seeds stay alive in soil for many years.

manas.q: Why is broomrape hard to control?

links.label: 📄 Source: Fernández-Aparicio et al. 2016, Frontiers in Plant Science

children.note: Long rotations with non-hosts, clean seed, solarisation, catch crops that trigger germination, later sowing and hand removal before seed set.

links.label: 📄 Source: Fernández-Aparicio et al. 2016, Frontiers in Plant Science

children.note: Introduced plants that spread fast and harm crops, pastures, people and animals.
An annual from the Americas now spreading in Kenya, Ethiopia and India; it cuts crop and pasture yields and causes skin allergy and asthma.

manas.q: What health problems does Parthenium cause?

links.label: 📄 Source: Adkins & Shabbir 2014, Pest Management Science

children.note: Uproot before flowering, plant competitive pastures or cover crops, and use the leaf beetle Zygogramma where approved as biocontrol.

links.label: 📄 Source: Adkins & Shabbir 2014, Pest Management Science

children.note: A thorny ornamental shrub that forms thickets, poisons livestock and releases allelopathic chemicals. Cutting alone fails; uproot at the root crown and replant cover.

links.label: 📄 Source: Bhagwat et al. 2012, PLoS ONE
📄 Source: Allelopathy of Lantana camara, Plants 2021

children.note: Wear gloves, long sleeves and a mask for Parthenium; bag flowering plants; never move seeding plants or infested soil; only hot-compost them before seed set.

manas.q: How should Parthenium be handled safely?

children.note: What is and is not allowed.
Glyphosate, atrazine and all synthetic herbicides are prohibited in certified organic production.

manas.q: Are synthetic herbicides allowed in organic farming?

children.note: Well-run organic fields combine prevention, timing and tools to stay clean; weedy fields usually mean late or missed weeding.
No single tool wins; combine rotation, cover, timely tillage and seed-bank control.

nodeData.note: Bees and other pollinators turn flowers into fruit and seed, and the same diverse habitat that feeds them also feeds the natural enemies of pests. Protecting them raises yields and quality, and beekeeping adds farm income.

children.note: Many fruit, vegetable, nut and seed crops need animals to move pollen; without them yields and fruit quality drop.
Of the leading global food crops, 87 depend on animal pollination to some degree, while staple cereals are wind- or self-pollinated.

manas.q: How many leading global food crops depend on animal pollination?
